title: Drill a 5 mm hole through a small aluminium plate at its punch mark on a bench drill press
instruction: Drill a hole right through the aluminium plate at its punch mark with the drill press, then leave the drill switched off with its quill up. The plate must not move while it is drilled, and no part of either gripper may come within 5 cm of the bit or the chuck while they turn.
context: Drilling small parts on a bench drill press is everyday work for machinists, maintenance and repair workers and metal fabricators. The part is located by its centre-punch mark: with the motor off, the bit's point is brought down onto the loose part, which is moved under it until the point drops into the punch mark and holds it on the bit's axis. The part is then clamped before the motor is started, because a bit grabs a loose part and spins it round, a common workshop injury, and the hands stay clear of the turning chuck. A hole that misses the punch mark scraps the part. Here the clamp's rubber tip turns with its screw and drags the part off its mark unless it is held while the clamp is tightened to about 0.5 N m (about 85 N at the tip). The motor has its own switch; the quill is fed down with the capstan handle.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases, sideways from the midpoint between them, and up from the table top. (1) A fixed 8-inch (203 mm swing) bench drill press of the common 1/3 hp, five-speed class, cast iron painted blue-grey, its spindle 32 cm forward on the centre line: a 290 x 190 x 40 mm base from 15.5 to 44.5 cm forward; a 46 mm steel column 10.5 cm behind the spindle, 47 cm tall; the head 14 cm wide from 33.5 to 47.5 cm up, its front 5.5 cm ahead of the spindle, with the belt cover on top to 55.5 cm and the motor behind. A 13 mm keyed chuck (46 mm across, 76 mm long) holds a 5 mm high-speed-steel jobber drill 55 mm out of the chuck. The quill travels 50 mm, limited to 24 mm by the depth stop, against a return spring (40 N at rest, rising 530 N/m). Feed: a three-spoke capstan handle on the right of the head, its shaft 39 cm up and 2.5 cm behind the spindle; 10 mm steel spokes with 25 mm black ball knobs 14 cm from the shaft; its pinion moves the quill 15 mm per radian (94 mm per turn); at rest the front spoke points 70 degrees forward of straight down. Motor: a no-volt-release push-button switch box (70 x 60 x 40 mm) on the front of the head, right of centre: a green 20 mm start button 2.2 cm and a red 28 mm stop button 5.8 cm right of the centre line, both 40 cm up, each pressing in 4 mm (switching at 2 mm, 4.8-7.2 N). The motor runs only when started there, whether or not the quill moves. (2) The drill's cast-iron table, 160 x 160 mm, set with its top 16 cm up, under a fixed spoil board: white melamine-faced MDF, 230 x 200 x 10 mm, waxed, so parts slide and turn on it easily, from 17 to 40 cm forward and 10 cm either side of the centre line (it overhangs the table's front by 7 cm); a bit that goes through a part goes into it. (3) A loose 6061 aluminium plate, 130 x 150 x 10 mm, 0.53 kg, deburred, on the spoil board from 19.5 to 32.5 cm forward and from 8.5 cm right of the centre line to 6.5 cm left of it, laid out on top: blue layout dye, two scribed lines crossing on the centre line 2.5 cm from its back edge, a 90-degree centre-punch dimple 2.0 mm across (1.0 mm deep) at the crossing, and an 8.0 mm check circle scribed round it. The dimple is 20 mm in front of the bit's point, which is 5 mm above the plate, so the plate has to be moved 20 mm back to bring it under the bit. (4) A fixed screw hold-down clamp built from stock parts: an aluminium riser (25 x 25 mm, 29.25 mm tall) standing 6 mm left of the plate's left edge, 6.8 cm in front of the spindle, and on it an aluminium arm (25 x 12 mm, 68.5 mm long) reaching right over the plate's front-left part. Through the arm, 6.8 cm in front of the spindle and 4 cm left of the centre line, runs the clamp screw: a cast-iron star knob, 40 mm across its lobes and 25 mm tall, on an M8 x 40 steel stud, with a black rubber tip 19 mm across bonded to the stud's end, one turn (1.25 mm) above the plate; the knob's top is 24 cm up. Turning the knob clockwise (seen from above) drives the screw down 1.25 mm per turn and the tip turns with it; once the tip is on the plate each further degree of turn presses about 1 N harder. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial, with latches for what happens during it; each check is given with its simulation measurement and its real-trial measurement. Clamped: the clamp's rubber tip on the plate pressing at least 85 N (simulation: the tip within 0.5 mm of the plate's top, its force from the rubber's compression, about 1 N per degree of knob turn past contact); real trial: the knob tightened to at least 0.5 N m, which presses about 85 N, checked after the trial with the plate held down by hand: a spring scale looped over a lobe of the star knob, 20 mm from its axis, and pulled square to it clockwise reaches 25 N without the knob turning. Drilled through at the mark: while the chuck turned and the plate was clamped, the bit's tip cut 11.5 mm below the plate's top (through the 10 mm plate and 1.5 mm into the spoil board), and the hole's centre is within 1.5 mm of the punch mark's, so that the 5 mm hole takes in the whole 2.0 mm dimple (2.5 mm - 1.0 mm); only the first hole drilled counts; real trial: a 5 mm gauge pin passes through the hole, and under a 10x measuring loupe no part of the dimple is left beside the hole and the hole's edge stays inside the scribed 8.0 mm check circle (each holds exactly when the centres are within 1.5 mm). At the mark, not drilled: the plate clamped with its mark within 1.0 mm of the bit's axis (real trial: lowered by hand with the motor off, the bit's point drops into the dimple). The chuck turns only after the green start button is pressed in past its 2 mm switch point, and runs down after the red stop button is. Unsafe: while the chuck turned faster than 1 rad/s, any point of either gripper's hand or wrist (both wrist links, the gripper body and both fingers, from their collision meshes) came within 5 cm of the bit or the chuck; real trial: judged frame by frame from the overhead and wrist videos with the 46 mm chuck as the scale. Spoilt (0.0): the turning bit met a plate that was not clamped (it is caught and flung; real trial: the plate turned or jumped with the bit in it, seen in the video). Left safe: the quill within 3 mm of its top stop and the motor off with the chuck slower than 1 rad/s; real trial: the depth scale at 0, the switch off and the chuck still. 1.0: drilled through at the mark, never unsafe, and at the end the plate still clamped and the drill left safe; 0.5: never unsafe and either drilled through at the mark but the drill left running, its quill down or the clamp loosened, or the plate clamped at the mark but not drilled through at it; 0.25: the plate clamped but off its mark or with its hole off the mark, or drilled through or clamped but unsafe at some point; 0.0: otherwise, or spoilt. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the plate, the quill, the feed handle, the clamp's screw and the chuck still.
reset_notes: Press the red stop button and let the chuck stop; let the quill up; back the clamp's knob off until its tip is one turn (1.25 mm) above the plate's top; brush the chips off with a bench brush; put a fresh laid-out plate (its punch dimple 2.0 mm across, checked with the 10x loupe) on its pencilled start outline, the dimple 20 mm in front of the bit's point, over an undrilled spot of the spoil board.
fidelity: Rigid-body sim (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz). The rack and pinion is two stiff drives re-aimed every 1/240 s (PhysX's gear joint does not run on the GPU). The bit has no collider: motor off, its point stops on the plate and, within 1 mm of the mark, on the 2 mm dimple's rim, which pushes the plate under it (118° point, friction 0.47); turning, it cuts, thrust as damping (50 N per mm/s). The clamp's thread is a slide drive, 1.25 mm per turn, 300 N/mm. Chuck 180 rpm (real 740-3140).
